# Independent Component Analysis {#sec-ica}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

Imagine standing in a crowded room where several people speak at once. Two microphones placed in different corners each pick up a different blend of all the voices. From those two mixed recordings, can you reconstruct what each individual speaker said? Your ear does something like this effortlessly, which is why the problem is known as the cocktail-party problem. Independent component analysis (ICA) is the statistical machinery that solves it without knowing anything about the voices or the room: it takes the mixed signals and pulls them back apart into the underlying sources.

This is a deceptively hard task. We never observe the original voices, and we do not know how they were combined. We only see the mixtures. The remarkable claim of ICA is that, under one structural assumption (the sources are statistically independent and at most one of them is Gaussian), the unmixing can be recovered up to harmless ambiguities of scale and ordering. The single idea that makes this possible is that mixing makes signals look more Gaussian, so undoing the mixing amounts to searching for directions in which the data look as non-Gaussian as possible.

ICA belongs to the same family of unsupervised, linear factorizations as principal components analysis (see @sec-dimension-reduction), and it is often introduced right after it. The two methods look superficially similar (both write the data as linear combinations of latent variables), but they optimize fundamentally different criteria. PCA seeks directions that are uncorrelated and capture maximal variance; ICA seeks directions that are statistically independent. As we will see, independence is a much stronger requirement than uncorrelatedness, and it is exactly what lets ICA separate sources that PCA cannot.

::: {.callout-important title="Key idea"}
PCA decorrelates (removes second-order, linear dependence) and orders directions by variance. ICA goes further and makes the recovered components statistically independent, which requires using information beyond the covariance matrix, namely the non-Gaussian structure of the data.
:::

## The Mixing Model {#sec-ica-model}

Let there be $m$ unobserved source signals collected into a random vector $\mathbf{s} = (s_1, \dots, s_m)^\top$. We observe $m$ mixtures $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_m)^\top$, each a linear combination of the sources. In matrix form the generative model is

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{s},
$$ {#eq-ica-mixing}

where $\mathbf{A}$ is an unknown invertible $m \times m$ mixing matrix. In the cocktail-party picture, $s_j$ is the $j$th speaker, $x_i$ is the $i$th microphone, and $A_{ij}$ encodes how loudly speaker $j$ reaches microphone $i$. Given a sample of $n$ observed vectors, stacked as the rows of an $n \times m$ matrix $\mathbf{X}$, the goal is to estimate an unmixing matrix $\mathbf{W} \approx \mathbf{A}^{-1}$ so that

$$
\hat{\mathbf{s}} = \mathbf{W}\,\mathbf{x}
$$ {#eq-ica-unmixing}

recovers the sources. The defining modelling assumption is that the components of $\mathbf{s}$ are mutually statistically independent,

$$
p_{\mathbf{s}}(s_1, \dots, s_m) = \prod_{j=1}^m p_j(s_j),
$$ {#eq-ica-indep}

and that at most one of the $p_j$ is Gaussian. We also assume the sources have zero mean (we can always center the data) and, without loss of generality, unit variance, because any scaling of a source can be absorbed into the corresponding column of $\mathbf{A}$.

::: {.callout-note title="The two unavoidable ambiguities"}
ICA can never recover the *scale* or the *order* of the sources. If $\mathbf{P}$ is a permutation matrix and $\mathbf{D}$ a nonzero diagonal matrix, then $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ mixing the rescaled, reordered sources $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{s}$ produces exactly the same observations $\mathbf{x}$. We fix scale by setting unit variance and accept that the labelling and the sign of each component are arbitrary. Everything else is identifiable.
:::

### Why independence and non-Gaussianity identify the sources {#sec-ica-identifiability}

The single deepest fact in ICA is that Gaussian sources cannot be separated, while non-Gaussian ones can. Understanding why explains the whole method.

Suppose the sources are jointly Gaussian, independent, with unit variance, so $\mathbf{s} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$. Then $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^\top)$. Now take any orthogonal matrix $\mathbf{Q}$ (so $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^\top = \mathbf{I}$) and define a rotated set of sources $\mathbf{s}' = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{s}$. Because the standard Gaussian is rotationally symmetric, $\mathbf{s}'$ is *also* $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ with independent components, and the alternative mixing matrix $\mathbf{A}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}^\top$ gives

$$
\mathbf{A}'\mathbf{s}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{Q}\,\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{x}.
$$ {#eq-ica-gauss-rotation}

The pair $(\mathbf{A}', \mathbf{s}')$ explains the data exactly as well as $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{s})$, and the two are not related by mere permutation and scaling. The model is unidentifiable: any rotation of jointly Gaussian sources is again valid independent Gaussian sources. Second-order statistics (the covariance) are all a Gaussian has, and the covariance is invariant to rotation, so there is simply no information left to pin down the rotation.

Non-Gaussian sources break this symmetry. To see how, consider any linear combination of the observed mixtures, $y = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{z}^\top \mathbf{s}$, where $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{w}$. So every candidate unmixing direction $\mathbf{w}$ produces an output $y$ that is a weighted sum of the independent sources, $y = \sum_j z_j s_j$. The classical central limit theorem says that sums of independent random variables tend toward a Gaussian. Therefore a generic mixture $\sum_j z_j s_j$ is *more Gaussian* than any single source. The output $y$ is least Gaussian precisely when the sum collapses onto a single source, that is, when $\mathbf{z}$ has exactly one nonzero entry. At that point $y$ equals one of the original $s_j$ (up to scale). This gives a constructive recipe:

> To recover a source, search over directions $\mathbf{w}$ for the one that makes $y = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}$ as far from Gaussian as possible.

Maximizing non-Gaussianity is the engine of ICA. Everything that follows is about how to measure "non-Gaussianity" with a tractable contrast function and how to optimize it efficiently.

## Whitening: Reducing the Problem to a Rotation {#sec-ica-whitening}

Before searching for the unmixing directions, it pays to preprocess the data so that the remaining work is as simple as possible. The preprocessing is whitening (also called sphering), and it is essentially the same linear-algebra step that powers PCA.

Center the observed data and compute the sample covariance $\mathbf{C} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top]$. Diagonalize it with its eigendecomposition $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{E}\,\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\,\mathbf{E}^\top$, where $\mathbf{E}$ holds the orthonormal eigenvectors and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m)$ the eigenvalues. Define the whitening matrix

$$
\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{E}\,\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\,\mathbf{E}^\top,
$$ {#eq-ica-whitener}

and the whitened data $\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{x}$. By construction $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ has identity covariance:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^\top]
= \mathbf{V}\,\mathbf{C}\,\mathbf{V}^\top
= \mathbf{E}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\mathbf{E}^\top \mathbf{E}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{E}^\top \mathbf{E}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\mathbf{E}^\top
= \mathbf{I}.
$$ {#eq-ica-white-cov}

Whitening removes all linear correlation and equalizes variance, which is exactly the second-order, PCA-level structure. What it cannot do is achieve independence, because that involves higher-order statistics. The crucial payoff is that, after whitening, the remaining mixing is a pure rotation. Writing $\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{s} = \tilde{\mathbf{A}}\,\mathbf{s}$ and using that $\mathbf{s}$ has identity covariance,

$$
\mathbf{I} = \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^\top]
= \tilde{\mathbf{A}}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{s}\mathbf{s}^\top]\,\tilde{\mathbf{A}}^\top
= \tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}^\top,
$$ {#eq-ica-orthogonal}

so $\tilde{\mathbf{A}}$ is orthogonal. The full unmixing problem ($m^2$ unknowns) has been reduced to finding an orthogonal matrix ($m(m-1)/2$ free parameters), which is just the search for the rotation that the identifiability argument said Gaussian data could never reveal but non-Gaussian data can. This is why ICA pipelines always whiten first: it halves the work and lets the contrast-function search operate on an orthonormal frame.

::: {.callout-tip title="Mental model"}
Whitening turns an arbitrary elliptical cloud into a spherical one. For Gaussian data the sphere looks the same from every angle, which is exactly why no rotation is special. For non-Gaussian data the sphere has lumpy, non-uniform structure, and ICA rotates the axes to line up with the lumps.
:::

## Measuring Non-Gaussianity: Contrast Functions {#sec-ica-contrast}

To turn "as non-Gaussian as possible" into an objective we can optimize, we need a scalar measure of how far a (zero-mean, unit-variance) random variable $y$ is from Gaussian. Two classical choices are kurtosis and negentropy.

### Kurtosis {#sec-ica-kurtosis}

The (excess) kurtosis of a zero-mean variable is

$$
\operatorname{kurt}(y) = \mathbb{E}[y^4] - 3\big(\mathbb{E}[y^2]\big)^2.
$$ {#eq-ica-kurtosis}

For a Gaussian, $\mathbb{E}[y^4] = 3(\mathbb{E}[y^2])^2$, so kurtosis is exactly zero; any nonzero value signals non-Gaussianity. Distributions with positive kurtosis are super-Gaussian (heavy-tailed, spiky, like speech or a Laplace density), while negative kurtosis indicates sub-Gaussian variables (flat-topped, like a uniform distribution or many digital signals). Kurtosis is attractive because it is simple and, for unit-variance variables, behaves nicely under linear combination: if $y = \sum_j z_j s_j$ with independent $s_j$ and $\sum_j z_j^2 = 1$, then

$$
\operatorname{kurt}(y) = \sum_{j=1}^m z_j^4 \,\operatorname{kurt}(s_j).
$$ {#eq-ica-kurt-additive}

Maximizing $|\operatorname{kurt}(y)|$ over the unit sphere $\sum_j z_j^2 = 1$ drives the weight onto a single coordinate (since the quartic $\sum z_j^4$ is maximized at a vertex), exactly recovering one source. The drawback is statistical: kurtosis depends on fourth moments and is therefore extremely sensitive to outliers, which can dominate the estimate. For this reason practitioners usually prefer negentropy with a robust nonlinearity.

### Negentropy {#sec-ica-negentropy}

Information theory offers the principled measure. Among all distributions with a fixed variance, the Gaussian has the largest differential entropy. So the *entropy gap* between $y$ and a Gaussian of the same variance is a natural, always-nonnegative measure of non-Gaussianity. This is negentropy:

$$
J(y) = H(y_{\text{gauss}}) - H(y),
\qquad H(y) = -\!\int p(u)\log p(u)\,du,
$$ {#eq-ica-negentropy}

where $y_{\text{gauss}}$ is Gaussian with the same variance as $y$. Negentropy is zero if and only if $y$ is Gaussian and positive otherwise, and unlike kurtosis it uses the entire distribution rather than a single moment, making it statistically well behaved. Its weakness is that it requires the unknown density $p$. The practical fix, due to Hyvarinen, is the approximation

$$
J(y) \approx \kappa \big(\mathbb{E}[G(y)] - \mathbb{E}[G(\nu)]\big)^2,
$$ {#eq-ica-negentropy-approx}

where $\nu \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, $\kappa > 0$ is a constant, and $G$ is a smooth, slowly growing nonquadratic function. Common choices are $G(u) = \tfrac{1}{a}\log\cosh(au)$ (so $g = G' = \tanh(au)$) and $G(u) = -e^{-u^2/2}$. These robust contrasts recover the spirit of kurtosis (the special case $G(u) = u^4$) while taming the sensitivity to tails, and they lead directly to the FastICA update.

## The FastICA Fixed-Point Algorithm {#sec-ica-fastica}

FastICA finds, on whitened data, a unit vector $\mathbf{w}$ that maximizes the negentropy approximation in @eq-ica-negentropy-approx. We derive its update rule, which is the centerpiece of practical ICA.

### Derivation of the fixed point {#sec-ica-fastica-derivation}

Work with whitened data $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ and write $y = \mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}}$. Maximizing the approximation in @eq-ica-negentropy-approx with respect to $\mathbf{w}$ is, up to constants and sign, the same as finding the stationary points of $\mathbb{E}[G(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})]$ subject to the unit-norm constraint $\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = 1$ (the constraint preserves unit variance because the data are whitened). Form the Lagrangian

$$
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}, \beta) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[G(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})\right] - \tfrac{\beta}{2}\big(\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 - 1\big).
$$ {#eq-ica-lagrangian}

Setting the gradient to zero, and writing $g = G'$, gives the stationarity condition

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\, g(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})\right] - \beta\,\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}.
$$ {#eq-ica-stationarity}

Denote the left side by $F(\mathbf{w})$. We solve $F(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0}$ with Newton's method, which needs the Jacobian. Differentiating,

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial \mathbf{w}}
= \mathbb{E}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^\top g'(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})\right] - \beta\,\mathbf{I}.
$$ {#eq-ica-jacobian}

Here comes the key approximation that gives FastICA its speed. Because the data are whitened, $\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^\top] = \mathbf{I}$, so we approximate the first term by factoring the expectation:

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^\top g'(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})\right]
\approx \mathbb{E}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^\top\right]\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[g'(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})\right]
= \mathbb{E}\!\left[g'(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})\right]\mathbf{I}.
$$ {#eq-ica-jac-approx}

The Jacobian becomes diagonal, $\big(\mathbb{E}[g'(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})] - \beta\big)\mathbf{I}$, so its inverse is trivial. The Newton step $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - (\partial F/\partial \mathbf{w})^{-1} F(\mathbf{w})$ reads

$$
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \frac{\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\,g(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})] - \beta\,\mathbf{w}}{\mathbb{E}[g'(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})] - \beta}.
$$ {#eq-ica-newton}

Multiplying through by the scalar $\beta - \mathbb{E}[g'(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})]$ (which only rescales $\mathbf{w}$, and we renormalize anyway) collapses this into the celebrated FastICA fixed-point update

$$
\mathbf{w}^{+} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\, g(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})\right] - \mathbb{E}\!\left[g'(\mathbf{w}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{x}})\right]\mathbf{w},
\qquad
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{w}^{+}}{\|\mathbf{w}^{+}\|}.
$$ {#eq-ica-fastica-update}

Each iteration evaluates a nonlinearity and two sample averages, then renormalizes; there is no step size to tune, and convergence is cubic near a solution, which is why the method is fast. With $g(u) = \tanh(au)$ we have $g'(u) = a\big(1 - \tanh^2(au)\big)$, the workhorse choice.

### Extracting all components {#sec-ica-deflation}

A single run of @eq-ica-fastica-update finds one independent component. To get them all, two schemes are used. In *deflation* (Gram-Schmidt) we extract components one at a time and, after each update, project out the directions already found,

$$
\mathbf{w}_p \leftarrow \mathbf{w}_p - \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} (\mathbf{w}_p^\top \mathbf{w}_j)\,\mathbf{w}_j,
\qquad
\mathbf{w}_p \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{w}_p}{\|\mathbf{w}_p\|},
$$ {#eq-ica-gram-schmidt}

so the new direction stays orthogonal to all previous ones (orthogonality in the whitened space is exactly the independence-preserving constraint from @eq-ica-orthogonal). In the *symmetric* scheme all rows of $\mathbf{W}$ are updated in parallel and then jointly orthogonalized via $\mathbf{W} \leftarrow (\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^\top)^{-1/2}\mathbf{W}$, which avoids the accumulation of error that deflation can suffer in the later components. The final unmixing matrix on the original data is $\hat{\mathbf{W}} = \mathbf{W}_{\text{white}}\,\mathbf{V}$, combining the learned rotation with the whitener of @eq-ica-whitener.

## ICA Versus PCA {#sec-ica-vs-pca}

It is worth stating the contrast with @sec-dimension-reduction sharply, because the two methods are so often confused.

| Aspect | PCA | ICA |
|---|---|---|
| Criterion | maximal variance | maximal independence (non-Gaussianity) |
| Statistics used | second order (covariance) | higher order (kurtosis, negentropy) |
| Output relation | uncorrelated, orthogonal | independent, generally non-orthogonal in data space |
| Ordering | by variance (meaningful) | none (arbitrary sign and order) |
| Goal | compression, denoising | source separation, latent structure |

: PCA and ICA optimize different things. {#tbl-ica-pca}

@tbl-ica-pca makes the central point: uncorrelated is not the same as independent. Independence implies uncorrelatedness, but the converse holds only for Gaussian variables. PCA stops at the covariance and therefore at uncorrelatedness; ICA exploits the non-Gaussian higher-order structure to reach full independence. A useful summary is that PCA does the whitening step of ICA (@sec-ica-whitening) and then stops, whereas ICA additionally finds the special rotation of the whitened data that lines the axes up with the independent sources. PCA is the right tool when the goal is to capture variance and compress; ICA is the right tool when the goal is to recover physically meaningful, independent generative factors.

## Assumptions, Properties, and Failure Modes {#sec-ica-properties}

A careful user should keep the following in mind.

- **Independence and non-Gaussianity are load-bearing.** If two or more sources are Gaussian, those sources occupy a subspace that ICA can identify but cannot resolve internally (the rotation within it is free, by @eq-ica-gauss-rotation). At most one Gaussian source is allowed. These are assumptions about the world, not about the algorithm, and they can be tested; @sec-ica-validity does so.
- **Sign, scale, and order are unidentifiable.** A recovered component can be flipped, rescaled, or relabelled relative to the true source. Downstream interpretation must account for this.
- **Square, noiseless model by default.** The basic model assumes as many mixtures as sources ($\mathbf{A}$ square and invertible) and no additive noise. Overcomplete ICA (more sources than sensors) and noisy ICA require richer estimators and are genuinely harder.
- **Complexity.** Whitening costs $O(nm^2 + m^3)$. Each FastICA iteration over $m$ components is $O(nm^2)$, and the fixed point typically converges in a handful of iterations, so ICA scales comfortably to large $n$ and moderate $m$.
- **Statistical conditioning.** Kurtosis-based contrasts are fragile to outliers; the robust $\log\cosh$ contrast (@sec-ica-negentropy) is the safer default. Convergence can land on a local optimum, so multiple random restarts are good practice.
- **Connections.** ICA is a maximum-likelihood method when the source densities are specified, and it can be read as a single-layer linear generative model. This links it to nonlinear and probabilistic latent-variable models such as autoencoders (@sec-autoencoders) and deep generative models (@sec-generative-models), which relax the linearity of @eq-ica-mixing. It is also a tool for unsupervised structure discovery alongside clustering (@sec-cluster) and density estimation (@sec-density-estimation).

::: {.callout-warning title="When ICA will disappoint you"}
ICA assumes instantaneous linear mixing. Real audio in a room involves echoes and delays (convolutive mixing), which the basic model does not capture; convolutive ICA or time-frequency methods are needed there. ICA also gives no inherent ranking of components, so do not expect the first recovered component to be the most important one.
:::

## Testing Whether the Independent Component Model Holds {#sec-ica-validity}

Everything in this chapter so far has *assumed* the model of @eq-ica-mixing and @eq-ica-indep. FastICA will happily return an unmixing matrix for any data you hand it, including data for which no linear unmixing into independent components exists. The recovered "sources" are then an artefact of the contrast function rather than a discovery about the world. @sec-ica-properties called the independence and non-Gaussianity assumptions load-bearing without saying how to check them; this section supplies the check, following @Hallin2026.

The difficulty is specific and worth naming. We cannot simply feed the estimated components $\hat{\mathbf{s}}$ to an off-the-shelf independence test, because $\hat{\mathbf{s}}$ was *chosen* to look as independent as possible. The estimation step has already used the data, so the null distribution of any naive statistic is wrong, and it is wrong in a way that depends both on which ICA estimator was used and on the unknown source distributions. @sec-ica-validity-reestimate shows by simulation just how wrong, because the effect is much larger than intuition suggests.

### The null hypothesis {#sec-ica-validity-null}

We are not testing whether a *particular* estimated unmixing is correct. We are testing whether the independent component model is true *at all*, that is, whether some linear representation of the observed vector into independent coordinates exists:

$$
\mathcal{H}_0:\quad \mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{s}
\ \ \text{for some } \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^m \text{ and invertible } \mathbf{A},
\ \text{with } s_1, \dots, s_m \text{ mutually independent.}
$$ {#eq-ica-null}

This is a statement about the *existence* of $(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{A})$, which is what makes it the right null: it is exactly the modelling assumption of @sec-ica-model, no more and no less. The alternative $\mathcal{H}_1$ is that no such pair exists, so that whatever FastICA returns cannot be a set of independent sources.

Two assumptions are needed, and both are mild.

**Assumption 1 (absolutely continuous observations).** The distribution of $\mathbf{x}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^m$.

*Reading.* No atoms, and no component confined to a lower-dimensional subspace. This is what gives the rank-based version below a tie-free null distribution. It is violated by discrete or heavily rounded measurements, and by data in which one variable is an exact linear function of the others.

**Assumption 2 (affine-equivariant unmixing estimator).** The estimator $\hat{\mathbf{W}}_n$ is affine equivariant: if the data are replaced by $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{c}$ for invertible $\mathbf{B}$, the estimated components change only by permutation and sign.

*Reading.* The estimator must not care about the units, centring, or orientation of the input. FOBI, JADE, and symmetric FastICA satisfy this; the deflation FastICA of @sec-ica-deflation does not exactly, because the extraction order depends on the starting values. This is the assumption most likely to be broken by a hand-rolled pipeline, and breaking it costs the invariance of @sec-ica-validity-invariance rather than the validity of the test.

### The test statistic {#sec-ica-validity-stat}

The statistic compares the joint distribution of the estimated components against the product of their marginals, and it does the comparison on characteristic functions rather than densities, which avoids having to choose a bandwidth for a density estimate.

Write the estimated components as $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_j = \hat{\mathbf{W}}_n(\mathbf{x}_j - \bar{\mathbf{x}})$ for $j = 1, \dots, n$, with $\hat{s}_{j\ell}$ the $\ell$th coordinate. Their joint empirical characteristic function and its $m$ marginals are

$$
\hat{\varphi}(\mathbf{t}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n e^{\,\mathrm{i}\,\mathbf{t}^\top \hat{\mathbf{s}}_j},
\qquad
\hat{\varphi}_\ell(t_\ell) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n e^{\,\mathrm{i}\,t_\ell \hat{s}_{j\ell}} .
$$ {#eq-ica-ecf}

Mutual independence of the coordinates is equivalent to the joint characteristic function factorizing into the product of the marginals at *every* $\mathbf{t}$ — this is the characteristic-function restatement of @eq-ica-indep, and it is an if-and-only-if, which is what makes the resulting test consistent. So the natural discrepancy is

$$
D_n(\mathbf{t}) = \hat{\varphi}(\mathbf{t}) - \prod_{\ell=1}^m \hat{\varphi}_\ell(t_\ell),
$$ {#eq-ica-discrepancy}

and the test statistic integrates its squared modulus against a weight:

$$
T_n = n \int_{\mathbb{R}^m} \big|D_n(\mathbf{t})\big|^2\, W(\mathbf{t})\, \mathrm{d}\mathbf{t},
\qquad
W(\mathbf{t}) = \prod_{\ell=1}^m w(t_\ell),
$$ {#eq-ica-Tn}

where $w$ is a symmetric probability density on $\mathbb{R}$. Large values of $T_n$ are evidence against @eq-ica-null. The weight is not a nuisance to be tolerated but the tuning knob of the procedure: it decides which frequencies $\mathbf{t}$ the test listens to, and hence which kinds of dependence it is most sensitive to. Taking $w$ with characteristic function

$$
\mathcal{C}(u) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{\,\mathrm{i}\,u t}\,w(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = e^{-\gamma u^{2}}, \qquad \gamma > 0,
$$ {#eq-ica-weight}

is the Gaussian member of the stable family used by @Hallin2026; small $\gamma$ spreads weight over high frequencies and picks up fine, local dependence, large $\gamma$ concentrates on low frequencies and picks up broad, global dependence.

### From an integral to a computable formula {#sec-ica-validity-closedform}

@eq-ica-Tn is an integral over $\mathbb{R}^m$, which looks unusable. It is not: the product structure of $W$ collapses it to a double sum. Expanding the squared modulus,

$$
\big|D_n(\mathbf{t})\big|^2
= \big|\hat{\varphi}(\mathbf{t})\big|^2
- 2\,\mathrm{Re}\Big[\hat{\varphi}(\mathbf{t}) \textstyle\prod_{\ell}\overline{\hat{\varphi}_\ell(t_\ell)}\Big]
+ \textstyle\prod_{\ell}\big|\hat{\varphi}_\ell(t_\ell)\big|^2,
$$ {#eq-ica-expand}

and each of the three pieces integrates in closed form. Write $\hat{s}_{jk,\ell} = \hat{s}_{j\ell} - \hat{s}_{k\ell}$ for the pairwise difference in coordinate $\ell$. For the first piece,

$$
n\!\int \big|\hat{\varphi}(\mathbf{t})\big|^2 W(\mathbf{t})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{t}
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j,k=1}^n \int e^{\,\mathrm{i}\,\mathbf{t}^\top(\hat{\mathbf{s}}_j - \hat{\mathbf{s}}_k)} \prod_\ell w(t_\ell)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{t}
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j,k=1}^n \prod_{\ell=1}^m \mathcal{C}\big(\hat{s}_{jk,\ell}\big),
$$ {#eq-ica-term1}

because the integral factorizes across coordinates and each factor is, by @eq-ica-weight, the characteristic function of $w$ evaluated at the difference. The third piece factorizes coordinate by coordinate from the start, giving $n\prod_{\ell}\big[n^{-2}\sum_{j,k}\mathcal{C}(\hat{s}_{jk,\ell})\big] = n^{1-2m}\prod_\ell \sum_{j,k}\mathcal{C}(\hat{s}_{jk,\ell})$. The cross piece separates the $j$ sum from $m$ inner $k$ sums, giving $-2n^{-m}\sum_j \prod_\ell \sum_k \mathcal{C}(\hat{s}_{jk,\ell})$; no real part survives because $w$ is symmetric, so $\mathcal{C}$ is real and even. Collecting the three,

$$
T_n
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j,k=1}^n \prod_{\ell=1}^m \mathcal{C}\big(\hat{s}_{jk,\ell}\big)
\;+\; \frac{1}{n^{2m-1}}\prod_{\ell=1}^m \sum_{j,k=1}^n \mathcal{C}\big(\hat{s}_{jk,\ell}\big)
\;-\; \frac{2}{n^{m}}\sum_{j=1}^n \prod_{\ell=1}^m \sum_{k=1}^n \mathcal{C}\big(\hat{s}_{jk,\ell}\big).
$$ {#eq-ica-Tn-closed}

Everything on the right is a sum over pairs of observations of a smooth kernel. Computationally this is $O(n^2 m)$, the same order as a distance-covariance statistic, and it involves no numerical integration, no density estimation, and no tuning beyond $\gamma$.

::: {.callout-note title="Why the statistic cannot go negative"}
@eq-ica-Tn-closed is an algebraic identity for a quantity *defined* as $n$ times the integral of a squared modulus against a non-negative weight. So $T_n \ge 0$ always, with equality only if the joint empirical characteristic function factorizes exactly. If a from-scratch implementation ever returns a negative value, the error is in the powers of $n$.
:::

### Affine invariance {#sec-ica-validity-invariance}

The test does not depend on the arbitrary choices of location, scale, and orientation in the data, and it is worth seeing where that comes from, because it is why Assumption 2 is stated as it is.

Location drops out first. If the components are estimated from uncentred data, every $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_j$ picks up a common shift $\mathbf{a}$, so every empirical characteristic function in @eq-ica-ecf is multiplied by $e^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{t}^\top \mathbf{a}}$; both terms of @eq-ica-discrepancy pick up the *same* unit-modulus factor, and $|D_n(\mathbf{t})|$ is unchanged. This is why no estimate of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ appears anywhere in @eq-ica-Tn-closed.

Scale and rotation drop out second, and here Assumption 2 does the work. Replace $\mathbf{x}_j$ by $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{c}$. An affine-equivariant estimator returns the *same* components up to a permutation and a sign flip — the two ambiguities of @sec-ica-model, which we already know are unavoidable. Because $W$ in @eq-ica-Tn is a product of identical factors, permuting coordinates permutes the factors and leaves the product alone; and flipping a sign leaves $\mathcal{C}(u) = e^{-\gamma u^2}$ alone because it is even. So $T_n$ is exactly unchanged. The test gives the same answer whether the microphones were calibrated in volts or millivolts, which is what one wants from a diagnostic for a model that is itself identified only up to scale and order.

### Calibration by permutation {#sec-ica-validity-perm}

The asymptotic null distribution of $T_n$ is an infinite weighted sum of $\chi^2_1$ variables whose weights depend on the unknown source densities *and* on which ICA estimator was used. It is not usable, so @Hallin2026 calibrates by resampling instead.

The first observation is that permuting *observations* does nothing: $T_n$ in @eq-ica-Tn-closed is symmetric in $j$, so shuffling rows returns the observed value exactly. What must be permuted is each *component* separately across observations. Fix coordinate $1$ and draw independent permutations $\sigma_2, \dots, \sigma_m$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, then form

$$
\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{*}_j = \big(\hat{s}_{j1},\, \hat{s}_{\sigma_2(j)2},\, \dots,\, \hat{s}_{\sigma_m(j)m}\big)^\top .
$$ {#eq-ica-perm}

This destroys any dependence *between* coordinates while leaving each marginal empirical distribution exactly intact, so $\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{*}$ is a sample from the product of the estimated marginals — a valid draw from $\mathcal{H}_0$.

The second observation is the one that is easy to miss, and @sec-ica-validity-reestimate shows what it costs to miss it. The permuted sample is a draw from the null *for the components*, but the observed statistic was computed on components that had been **estimated**. To compare like with like, each permuted sample must be passed back through the same estimator before the statistic is recomputed:

$$
T_n^{*} = T_n\big(\hat{\mathbf{W}}^{*}\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{*}\big),
\qquad \hat{\mathbf{W}}^{*} = \text{the unmixing estimated from } \hat{\mathbf{s}}^{*} .
$$ {#eq-ica-perm-reest}

Repeating for $B$ permutations gives the $p$-value

$$
\hat{p} = \frac{1 + \#\{b : T_n^{*(b)} \ge T_n\}}{B + 1},
$$ {#eq-ica-pvalue}

which is valid at any level of the form $\lfloor \alpha(B+1)\rfloor/(B+1)$ without asymptotics and without knowing the source distributions.

A rank-scored variant strengthens this further. Replace each estimated component by a score of its within-column rank,

$$
\tilde{s}_{j\ell} = J\!\left(\frac{R_{j\ell}}{n+1}\right),
\qquad R_{j\ell} = \text{rank of } \hat{s}_{j\ell} \text{ among } \hat{s}_{1\ell}, \dots, \hat{s}_{n\ell},
$$ {#eq-ica-ranks}

with a score function $J$ — the normal-quantile (van der Waerden) score $J = \Phi^{-1}$ is the default — and compute @eq-ica-Tn-closed from $\tilde{s}$. Ranks strip away the marginal distributions entirely, so the null distribution no longer depends on them, and the statistic inherits the robustness to heavy tails that @sec-ica-kurtosis warned ICA contrasts otherwise lack. The conventional expectation is that this costs power, since information in the marginals is discarded; @tbl-ica-validity-power shows that on this data-generating process it does not, which is a reminder that the trade is not automatic.

### Consistency {#sec-ica-validity-consistency}

Let $D(\mathbf{t})$ be the population analogue of @eq-ica-discrepancy, built from the characteristic function of the components at the estimator's probability limit. Under $\mathcal{H}_1$ no affine map makes the coordinates independent, so $D(\mathbf{t}) \not\equiv 0$; since $D$ is continuous and $W$ is strictly positive on all of $\mathbb{R}^m$, the integral $\int |D(\mathbf{t})|^2 W(\mathbf{t})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{t}$ is strictly positive. Because $n^{-1}T_n$ converges in probability to that integral, $T_n \to \infty$ while the permutation critical values stay bounded in probability, so the test rejects with probability tending to one. That is the "consistent" of the paper's title, and it is a strong statement: no dependence structure, however exotic, escapes detection given enough data. The strict positivity of $W$ is what buys it, which is the technical reason the weight must be a density with full support rather than a compactly supported kernel.

::: {.callout-important title="Key idea"}
The estimation step is not corrected for; it is absorbed. Because the statistic is affine-invariant and the critical values come from re-running the whole estimate-then-test pipeline on permuted components, the test is valid *whatever* the ICA estimator did, provided that estimator was affine equivariant.
:::

### Implementation {#sec-ica-validity-code}

We implement @eq-ica-Tn-closed and the calibration of @eq-ica-perm-reest from scratch, in the same spirit as the from-scratch fixed point of @sec-ica-fastica.

The unmixing estimator has to satisfy Assumption 2, so we use FOBI rather than the deflation FastICA built earlier: FOBI whitens and then diagonalizes the fourth-order scatter matrix $\mathbb{E}\big[\|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\|^2\,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^\top\big]$ in closed form, which is affine equivariant by construction and has no starting values to worry about.

```{r}
#| label: ica-validity-setup

## --- FOBI: a closed-form, affine-equivariant ICA estimator --------------
fobi_unmix <- function(X) {
  X  <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
  e  <- eigen(cov(X), symmetric = TRUE)
  V  <- e$vectors %*% diag(1 / sqrt(e$values), nrow(e$vectors)) %*% t(e$vectors)
  Xw <- X %*% V                                        # whitened (eq. ica-whitener)
  B  <- crossprod(Xw * sqrt(rowSums(Xw^2))) / nrow(Xw) # E[||x||^2 x x^T]
  scale(Xw %*% eigen(B, symmetric = TRUE)$vectors, TRUE, TRUE)
}

## --- van der Waerden scores of eq. ica-ranks ---------------------------
vdw <- function(Z) apply(Z, 2, function(z) qnorm(rank(z) / (length(z) + 1)))

## --- the statistic of eq. ica-Tn-closed --------------------------------
icm_stat <- function(Z, gamma = 1) {
  n <- nrow(Z); m <- ncol(Z)
  M <- lapply(seq_len(m), function(l) exp(-gamma * outer(Z[, l], Z[, l], "-")^2))
  sum(Reduce(`*`, M)) / n +
    prod(vapply(M, sum, 0)) / n^(2 * m - 1) -
    2 * sum(Reduce(`*`, lapply(M, rowSums))) / n^m
}

## --- comparator: distance covariance (m = 2) ---------------------------
dcov_stat <- function(Z) {
  dcen <- function(v) {
    D <- abs(outer(v, v, "-"))
    D - rowMeans(D)[row(D)] - colMeans(D)[col(D)] + mean(D)
  }
  sum(dcen(Z[, 1]) * dcen(Z[, 2]))
}

## --- permutation of components, eq. ica-perm ---------------------------
perm_cols <- function(Z) {
  for (l in 2:ncol(Z)) Z[, l] <- Z[sample.int(nrow(Z)), l]
  Z
}

## --- correct calibration: permute, RE-ESTIMATE, recompute (eq. ica-perm-reest)
perm_test <- function(Z, stat, B = 99, ranks = FALSE) {
  T0 <- stat(if (ranks) vdw(Z) else Z)
  Tp <- replicate(B, {
    Zp <- fobi_unmix(perm_cols(Z))          # <- the re-estimation step
    stat(if (ranks) vdw(Zp) else Zp)
  })
  (1 + sum(Tp >= T0)) / (B + 1)
}

## --- naive calibration: permute the estimated components and stop ------
naive_test <- function(Z, stat, B = 99) {
  T0 <- stat(Z)
  Tp <- replicate(B, stat(perm_cols(Z)))
  (1 + sum(Tp >= T0)) / (B + 1)
}
```

The comparator deserves a word. @Hallin2026 benchmarks against a distance-covariance test in the spirit of @Matteson2017, which measures dependence through pairwise distances rather than characteristic functions. We give it the *same* calibration, so that the only thing being compared is the dependence measure itself.

For the data-generating process we need components that are independent under the null, dependent under the alternative in a way no linear map can remove, and — a requirement that turns out to matter a great deal, see @sec-ica-validity-pitfalls — of clearly *different* kurtosis, so that FOBI's fourth-order eigenvalues are separated and the unmixing is identified. A Clayton copula with one exponential margin (excess kurtosis $+6$) and one uniform margin (excess kurtosis $-1.2$) does all three. The copula parameter $\theta$ indexes the violation: at $\theta = 0$ the components are independent and $\mathcal{H}_0$ holds exactly, and for $\theta > 0$ the dependence grows.

```{r}
#| label: ica-validity-dgp

A_mix <- matrix(c(1, 1, 0.5, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)   # as in fig-ica-signals

gen_clayton <- function(n, theta) {
  u1 <- runif(n); w <- runif(n)
  u2 <- if (theta <= 0) runif(n) else                      # theta = 0 is independence
    (u1^(-theta) * (w^(-theta / (1 + theta)) - 1) + 1)^(-1 / theta)
  cbind(qexp(u1) - 1, u2 - 0.5) %*% t(A_mix)               # kurtoses +6 and -1.2
}
```

### Why the components must be re-estimated {#sec-ica-validity-reestimate}

Before looking at power, it is worth paying for the lesson that the re-estimation step in @eq-ica-perm-reest is not a technicality. We compare the two calibrations on data where $\mathcal{H}_0$ holds exactly, so both should reject $5\%$ of the time.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ica-validity-calibration
#| tbl-cap: "Empirical size at the 5% level under the null (theta = 0), 100 replications, B = 99. The naive calibration permutes the estimated components and stops; the correct one passes each permuted sample back through FOBI before recomputing the statistic. The naive test is badly anti-conservative, and gets worse as n grows."

set.seed(99)
R <- 100; B <- 99; alpha <- 0.05

calib <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(150, 300), function(n) {
  s <- replicate(R, {
    Z <- fobi_unmix(gen_clayton(n, 0))
    c(naive_test(Z, icm_stat, B), perm_test(Z, icm_stat, B))
  })
  data.frame(n = n,
             naive = mean(s[1, ] <= alpha),
             `re-estimated` = mean(s[2, ] <= alpha),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(calib, row.names = FALSE)
```

@tbl-ica-validity-calibration is worth staring at. The naive test rejects far more often than it should, and the problem *worsens* with the sample size rather than washing out. The reason is that FOBI recovers the unmixing with an error of order $n^{-1/2}$, so each estimated component is a slight blend of both true sources; blending two independent sources makes the estimates genuinely dependent, by an amount of order $n^{-1/2}$. Since @eq-ica-Tn multiplies by $n$, that contribution is $O(1)$ and never vanishes. The permuted samples, which are never passed through the estimator, carry no such blending, so the observed statistic sits systematically above them. Re-estimating inside the loop puts the same blending into every replicate, and the size comes back to nominal up to Monte Carlo error — with $R = 100$ replications the standard error at a true $5\%$ is about $2$ percentage points.

### Size and power {#sec-ica-validity-sim}

Now the study proper: 100 replications at each of two sample sizes and four values of $\theta$, with $B = 99$ permutations and a nominal level of $5\%$. The $\theta = 0$ rows are size; the rest is power. (This chunk is a genuine Monte Carlo study and takes some minutes to run.)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ica-validity-power
#| tbl-cap: "Rejection rates at the 5% level over 100 replications, B = 99. CF is the characteristic-function test of eq. ica-Tn-closed, CF-rank its van der Waerden version, dCov the distance-covariance comparator; all three use the re-estimating calibration of eq. ica-perm-reest. The theta = 0 rows are empirical size, the rest power against Clayton dependence that no linear unmixing can remove."

set.seed(2026)
R <- 100; B <- 99; alpha <- 0.05
grid <- expand.grid(n = c(150, 300), theta = c(0, 0.5, 1, 2))

power_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  n <- grid$n[i]; th <- grid$theta[i]
  p <- replicate(R, {
    Z <- fobi_unmix(gen_clayton(n, th))
    c(perm_test(Z, icm_stat, B),
      perm_test(Z, icm_stat, B, ranks = TRUE),
      perm_test(Z, dcov_stat, B))
  })
  data.frame(theta = th, n = n,
             CF        = mean(p[1, ] <= alpha),
             `CF-rank` = mean(p[2, ] <= alpha),
             dCov      = mean(p[3, ] <= alpha),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(power_tab[order(power_tab$theta, power_tab$n), ], row.names = FALSE)
```

Read the $\theta = 0$ rows first. The raw characteristic-function test and the distance-covariance comparator both sit at the nominal $5\%$, which is the calibration of @eq-ica-perm-reest doing its job even though the components were estimated from the same data. The rank version runs a little liberal; with $R = 100$ replications the Monte Carlo standard error at a true $5\%$ is about $2$ percentage points, so this is at the edge of what the noise explains, and its power numbers below should be read with that in mind.

Then read down the $\theta$ column: power rises with the strength of the violation and with $n$, and by $\theta = 2$ all three tests are essentially certain to catch a model that does not hold. Between $\theta = 0.5$ and $\theta = 1$ the differences are large, and this is where the honest result of the exercise sits.

::: {.callout-note title="What this simulation does not reproduce"}
@Hallin2026 reports that the characteristic-function statistic substantially outperforms the distance-covariance test of @Matteson2017. **On this data-generating process it does not.** Distance covariance beats the plain characteristic-function test at every alternative here, and the van der Waerden version beats it too.

That disagreement is a fact about this one experiment, not a refutation of the paper, and the reasons are worth being explicit about. We fix a single dependence structure (a Clayton copula on two coordinates), a single weight function, and a single untuned $\gamma = 1$, whereas the published study varies the weight family and its parameter, the dependence structure, the dimension, and the ICA estimator; and $\gamma$ is exactly the knob that decides which frequencies the statistic listens to (@sec-ica-validity-stat), so a fixed choice can easily be mismatched to a particular alternative. The lesson to carry away is the practical one from @sec-ica-validity-practice: the characteristic-function test buys consistency, affine invariance, and a valid finite-sample level, but its *power* depends on a weight you have to choose, and against a specific alternative a tuning-free competitor may well do better.
:::

### Where the test does not help {#sec-ica-validity-failure}

Two limits are worth seeing, and the second is the more important.

The first is ordinary: against a weak violation at a small sample size the test has little power, as the $\theta = 0.5$, $n = 150$ row of @tbl-ica-validity-power shows. Failing to reject is not evidence that the model holds.

The second is structural, and no amount of data removes it. Suppose the sources really are independent but *both Gaussian*. Then $\mathcal{H}_0$ of @eq-ica-null is true — independent components do exist — so the test should reject only at the nominal rate, and it does. But by @eq-ica-gauss-rotation those components are not identified: every rotation of them is an equally valid set of independent Gaussian sources, and FOBI returns an essentially arbitrary one.

```{r}
#| label: ica-validity-gaussian

set.seed(7)
gauss_rej <- mean(replicate(100, {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(2 * 300), ncol = 2) %*% t(A_mix)   # two Gaussian sources
  perm_test(fobi_unmix(X), icm_stat, B = 99)
}) <= 0.05)

data.frame(n = 300, replications = 100, rejection_rate = gauss_rej)
```

The test passes the Gaussian data, correctly, because the independent component *model* is true. What it cannot tell you is that the components it passed are meaningless: no rotation of them is any more the "right" one than any other. A model can be valid and its estimate still carry no information.

::: {.callout-warning title="A pass is not a licence to interpret"}
The test validates the *model* of @eq-ica-null, not the *estimate*. Two or more Gaussian sources sail through it while leaving the recovered components completely unidentified (@eq-ica-gauss-rotation). Always pair the test with a check that at most one component is close to Gaussian — a normality test, or a glance at the estimated kurtoses of @eq-ica-kurtosis — before attaching meaning to any individual component.
:::

### Practical guidance {#sec-ica-validity-practice}

- **Where it belongs.** Run it as step 5 of @sec-ica-howto, after fitting and before interpreting.
- **Cost.** The statistic is $O(n^2 m)$ and the calibration re-runs the estimator $B$ times, so a test costs roughly $B$ times one fit plus $B$ statistic evaluations. That is seconds at $n$ in the hundreds and worth budgeting for at $n$ in the tens of thousands.
- **Software.** The CRAN package `TICM` [@TICM] implements the full family — several weight functions, both permutation and bootstrap calibration, and the rank versions — with the unmixing supplied by `JADE` or `fICA`. Its main function is also called `icm_test`; the from-scratch code above is deliberately named `perm_test` and `icm_stat` to keep the two apart, and covers only the Gaussian weight with $m = 2$.

```{r}
#| label: ica-validity-ticm
#| eval: false

# install.packages("TICM")
library(TICM)

# X is the n x m matrix of observed mixtures.
res <- icm_test(X, n.rep = 200, weight = "Gauss", ica = "JADE")
plot(res)   # scatterplot matrix of the estimated components

# ind_test() is the companion that tests independence of raw coordinates with
# no unmixing step. See ?icm_test for the score, weight, and strategy options.
```

- **Choosing $\gamma$.** Report more than one. The test is valid for any fixed $\gamma > 0$, so the honest practice is to run a small grid, say $\gamma \in \{0.5, 1, 2\}$, and report the range of $p$-values rather than searching for the $\gamma$ that rejects.
- **Number of permutations.** $B = 99$ suffices for a decision at $5\%$; use $B = 999$ if you intend to report the $p$-value itself, and remember @eq-ica-pvalue cannot return anything below $1/(B+1)$.
- **Dimension.** The statistic is a product over $m$ coordinates, and products of many numbers in $(0,1)$ underflow. Beyond moderate $m$, work on the log scale or reduce dimension with PCA first, as step 2 of @sec-ica-howto already recommends.

### Pitfalls {#sec-ica-validity-pitfalls}

- **Skipping the re-estimation.** The costliest error, and invisible unless you check the size: see @tbl-ica-validity-calibration.
- **Permuting rows instead of columns.** $T_n$ is symmetric in $j$, so shuffling observations returns the observed value every time and the $p$-value collapses to $1$. Permute each component separately, as in @eq-ica-perm.
- **Sources with equal kurtosis.** FOBI separates components by the *eigenvalues* of the fourth-order scatter matrix, so two sources with the same kurtosis leave those eigenvalues tied and the rotation unidentified — FOBI then returns an arbitrary blend, and the test rejects a model that is perfectly true. This is a defect of the estimator, not of the test, and it is why the simulation above pairs an exponential margin with a uniform one. JADE, which uses the full set of fourth-order cumulant matrices, is more robust here; if you suspect near-equal kurtoses, use it.
- **Using a non-equivariant estimator.** Deflation FastICA with random restarts breaks Assumption 2, and the test then answers a question about your starting values as well as about the data.
- **Reading non-rejection as confirmation.** With the Gaussian case above as the extreme illustration, the test is a filter that removes clearly invalid applications, not a certificate of validity.

## Practical How-To {#sec-ica-howto}

A reliable ICA workflow looks like this.

1. **Center** the data (subtract the column means) and, if features are on very different scales, consider standardizing.
2. **Choose the number of components.** With noise or many sensors, first reduce dimension with PCA (@sec-dimension-reduction), keeping the leading components, then run ICA on that subspace. This both denoises and sets $m$.
3. **Whiten** using @eq-ica-whitener.
4. **Run FastICA** with a robust nonlinearity ($\tanh$ by default), using the symmetric orthogonalization (@sec-ica-deflation) and several random initializations.
5. **Test the model before you trust it.** Run the validity test of @sec-ica-validity. If it rejects, no linear unmixing into independent components exists and the output of step 4 is an artefact of the contrast function rather than a set of recovered sources.
6. **Interpret with care.** Fix signs and an ordering by a convention that suits the application (for example, order by the variance the component explains in the original data, or by kurtosis), and remember these choices are arbitrary.

In R the `fastICA` package implements all of this. For transparency the demonstration below also includes a from-scratch fixed-point implementation so the mechanics of @eq-ica-fastica-update are fully visible.

## A Runnable Demonstration {#sec-ica-demo}

We generate two non-Gaussian sources, a square wave and a sawtooth, mix them linearly, and recover them with a from-scratch FastICA built directly from the equations above. The square and sawtooth are deliberately sub-Gaussian, so their mixtures are visibly more bell-shaped, which is the non-Gaussianity that ICA exploits.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ica-signals
#| fig-cap: "Two independent source signals (square wave and sawtooth) and the two linear mixtures actually observed. The mixtures interleave both sources, and neither row of the mixtures resembles a clean source."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

set.seed(1)
n  <- 2000
tt <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)

s1 <- sign(sin(2 * pi * 5 * tt))     # square wave
s2 <- 2 * ((tt * 7) %% 1) - 1        # sawtooth in [-1, 1]
S  <- cbind(s1, s2)
S  <- scale(S, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)   # center the sources

A  <- matrix(c(1, 1, 0.5, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)  # mixing matrix
X  <- S %*% t(A)                                        # observed mixtures

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1), mgp = c(1.8, 0.6, 0))
plot(tt, S[, 1], type = "l", main = "Source 1 (square)",   xlab = "time", ylab = "")
plot(tt, S[, 2], type = "l", main = "Source 2 (sawtooth)", xlab = "time", ylab = "")
plot(tt, X[, 1], type = "l", main = "Mixture 1 (observed)", xlab = "time", ylab = "")
plot(tt, X[, 2], type = "l", main = "Mixture 2 (observed)", xlab = "time", ylab = "")
par(op)
```

@fig-ica-signals shows the latent sources and the mixtures we actually get to see. Now we whiten and run the fixed-point iteration of @eq-ica-fastica-update with the $\tanh$ nonlinearity, extracting both components by deflation (@eq-ica-gram-schmidt).

```{r}
#| label: ica-fit

# --- whitening (eq. ica-whitener) ---
whiten <- function(Z) {
  Z  <- sweep(Z, 2, colMeans(Z))         # center
  e  <- eigen(cov(Z), symmetric = TRUE)  # eigendecomposition of covariance
  V  <- e$vectors %*% diag(1 / sqrt(e$values)) %*% t(e$vectors)
  list(Zw = Z %*% V, V = V)
}

# --- one FastICA unit via the fixed-point update (eq. fastica-update) ---
fastica_one <- function(Xw, w, others, iters = 300, tol = 1e-10) {
  w <- w / sqrt(sum(w^2))
  for (i in seq_len(iters)) {
    wx   <- as.vector(Xw %*% w)
    g    <- tanh(wx)                      # g  = G'
    gp   <- 1 - tanh(wx)^2                # g' = G''
    wnew <- colMeans(Xw * g) - mean(gp) * w
    if (length(others))                  # deflation: orthogonalize (eq. gram-schmidt)
      for (k in seq_along(others)) wnew <- wnew - sum(wnew * others[[k]]) * others[[k]]
    wnew <- wnew / sqrt(sum(wnew^2))
    if (1 - abs(sum(wnew * w)) < tol) { w <- wnew; break }
    w <- wnew
  }
  w
}

wh <- whiten(X)
Xw <- wh$Zw
W  <- list()
for (j in 1:2) {
  set.seed(10 + j)
  W[[j]] <- fastica_one(Xw, rnorm(2), W)
}
Wm   <- do.call(rbind, W)
Shat <- Xw %*% t(Wm)        # estimated sources

# recovery quality: best absolute correlation with a true source
recov <- c(max(abs(cor(Shat[, 1], S))),
           max(abs(cor(Shat[, 2], S))))
round(recov, 3)
```

The recovered components match the true sources almost perfectly (absolute correlations near one), confirming that the fixed point of @eq-ica-fastica-update has separated the mixtures. @fig-ica-recovered plots them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ica-recovered
#| fig-cap: "Sources recovered by the from-scratch FastICA. Up to an arbitrary sign and ordering (the two unavoidable ICA ambiguities), the square wave and sawtooth are cleanly separated from the mixtures."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.6

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1), mgp = c(1.8, 0.6, 0))
plot(tt, Shat[, 1], type = "l", main = "Recovered component 1", xlab = "time", ylab = "")
plot(tt, Shat[, 2], type = "l", main = "Recovered component 2", xlab = "time", ylab = "")
par(op)
```

For everyday use the `fastICA` package wraps the whitening, the symmetric fixed point, and component extraction into one call. The following reproduces the separation in a single line (it uses the same algorithm we built by hand).

```{r}
#| label: ica-package
#| eval: false

# install.packages("fastICA")
library(fastICA)
fit  <- fastICA(X, n.comp = 2, fun = "logcosh", method = "C")
Shat <- fit$S   # estimated independent components, one per column
```

The contrast between this chapter and @sec-dimension-reduction is the whole lesson in miniature: PCA would have whitened these mixtures and stopped, leaving two uncorrelated but still mixed signals; ICA found the extra rotation that the non-Gaussianity of the sources made identifiable, and so pulled the voices apart.
